citation: Fowler, C. (2015). Virtual reality and learning: Where is the pedagogy? British Journal of Educational Technology, 46(2), 412–422. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.12135 [version of record 2015; online-first © 2014]
thesis: Dalgarno and Lee's influential model of learning in 3-D virtual learning environments is technology-led — it derives learning benefits from technical affordances rather than starting from pedagogy — so Fowler extends it with a pedagogical layer, 'pedagogical immersion' drawn from Mayes and Fowler's (1999) three-stage framework, yielding a combined model anchored on Intended Learning Outcomes and a 'design for learning' process; the paper is a conceptual call-to-arms, not an empirical test.

sections.title: Abstract / framing
sections.summary: States the extension aim: build a more pedagogical description of Dalgarno and Lee's model using 'pedagogical immersion' from Mayes and Fowler's framework, adopting a 'design for learning' perspective.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Opens from Mikropoulos and Natsis's (2011) finding that most VR-in-education studies lack an explicit pedagogical model; frames Dalgarno and Lee (2010) as valuable but technology-led, motivating extension rather than rejection.

sections.title: Dalgarno and Lee's (2010) model of learning in 3-D VWs
sections.summary: Restates the source model's characteristics (representational fidelity, learner interaction), emergent properties (presence, co-presence, identity construction), and five learning affordances; introduces two critical seams — an inverted-U (Yerkes-Dodson) challenge to the fidelity/interaction-to-learning assumption, and the claim that presence/co-presence/identity describe antecedents rather than the learning experience itself.

sections.title: Extending the model
sections.summary: Introduces Mayes and Fowler's (1999) conceptualisation/construction/dialogue stages; proposes 'immersion' as bridge concept between technology and pedagogy; distinguishes conceptual/task/social immersion, renamed empathy/reification/identification; assembles the combined model anchored on Intended Learning Outcomes (Biggs, 2003) and a 'design for learning' process via Bloom's revised taxonomy (Anderson et al., 2001) and Conole et al.'s (2004) mini-learning activities.

sections.title: Further research
sections.summary: Calls for empirical validation of both frameworks, applied requirements-elicitation research, comparative designs holding pedagogy or technology constant (citing Clark's 1994 media-vs-method debate), and new design guidelines for educational VLEs.

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: restated directly from Dalgarno & Lee as display-quality/realism characteristic; visual realism, object-behavior consistency, communication realism, user-representation quality

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: restated as 'learner interaction'; richness of interaction resulting mainly from degree of embodiment

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: avatar discussion — user's representation able to communicate, show emotion, control/create objects

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: restated as emergent psychological property of fidelity x interaction; critiqued as an antecedent of, not identical to, the learning experience

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: restated as multi-user emergent property ('sense of being there together'); same antecedent-not-experience critique applied

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: reworked as bridge concept between technology and pedagogy; paired with a distinct, non-cluster-row pedagogical-immersion sense

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: one of Dalgarno & Lee's five affordances; recast in Fowler's own apparatus as a 'generic' design-for-learning requirement

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: via 'contextual learning' affordance and Fowler's own ILO / Bloom's-revised-taxonomy knowledge-dimension mapping

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: Table 1's 'dialogue' stage; skill-acquisition and real-world-performance objectives mapped to Conole et al.'s mini-learning activities

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.design: no original empirical study; this is Dalgarno & Lee's (and Fowler's own) scope-defining object throughout — standard-PC-explorable 3-D VLEs, explicitly distinguished from immersive/CAVE systems

conditions.label: SEM / process model (no media contrast)
conditions.design: secondary citation of Lee, Wong & Fung (2010), an SEM study distinguishing input/mediating/moderating/output variables; cited approvingly for its 'process' approach but flagged as non-immersive and avatar-free, so unable to test embodiment/immersion claims

readings.claim: Dalgarno and Lee's model, despite its influence, is technology-led — deriving learning benefits from technical affordances rather than starting from pedagogical requirements.

The assumption that higher representational fidelity and richer learner interaction straightforwardly produce deeper learning is questionable; an inverted-U (Yerkes-Dodson) relationship is more plausible, and some contexts may not need the fidelity/interaction continuum considered at all.
Presence, co-presence, and identity construction describe antecedents of a learning experience, not the experience itself.
'Immersion' can bridge technology, psychology, and pedagogy because a pedagogical sense of immersion (interaction of pedagogical variables) parallels the technical sense (fidelity x interaction).

Mayes and Fowler's three learning stages correspond to three renamed immersion-types — empathy (conceptual), reification (task), identification (social) — chosen to sit terminologically alongside Dalgarno and Lee's construction-of-identity/presence/co-presence triad.

The combined model anchors both frameworks on Intended Learning Outcomes and yields a 'design for learning' process from learning stage through learning objective, learning activity, and learning specification, modulated by contextual variables.
'Design for learning' is distinguished from 'learning design' (the IMS-LD/EML formal-specification tradition): the former is holistic and outcomes-oriented, the latter a specification language.
Future comparative research should isolate pedagogy's and technology's separate contributions by holding one constant while varying the other, controlling for novelty and placebo effects.

tensions.axis: extension of Dalgarno & Lee vs. contestation of Dalgarno & Lee
tensions.note: Fowler's stated aim is extension (retains the full affordance apparatus), but two moves genuinely contest the source: the inverted-U challenge to 'more fidelity/interaction = more learning,' and the claim that presence/co-presence/identity describe antecedents rather than the learning experience itself.
Fowler's central diagnostic axis for the whole VR-in-education field, not only Dalgarno & Lee; Mayes & Fowler's framework is offered as the pedagogy-led counterexample.

tensions.axis: immersion as technological property vs. immersion as pedagogical property
tensions.note: Fowler's own terminological innovation — a second, non-technical sense of 'immersion' parallel to the fidelity x interaction sense — flagged as a source of potential ambiguity he tries to resolve by renaming the pedagogical instances empathy/reification/identification.

tensions.axis: media-comparison research vs. method-held-constant research (Clark's media-vs-method debate)
tensions.note: Fowler sides with the method-not-media position for future research design, cautioning against studies that vary technology without controlling for pedagogy or vice versa.
